How to Get Rid of Bed Bugs — What Actually Works (2024)

By Shaw's Pest Control  ·  Wichita, KS

How to Get Rid of Bed Bugs: What Actually Works

If you're searching for how to get rid of bed bugs, you're likely dealing with an infestation right now—and you need answers that work, not theories. Bed bugs are resilient pests that have developed resistance to many over-the-counter treatments, making DIY elimination difficult and often unsuccessful. Shaw's Pest Control has been treating bed bug infestations across Wichita and surrounding Kansas communities since 1987, and our Master Tech-certified technicians have seen firsthand what eliminates these pests permanently versus what wastes time and money. This guide explains the proven methods for bed bug elimination, what research shows about DIY success rates, and how to prepare your home for professional treatment that actually works.

Why Bed Bugs Are So Hard to Eliminate

Bed bugs survive because they've evolved exceptional hiding abilities and impressive resistance to common pesticides. Adult bed bugs are about the size of an apple seed, but their eggs are microscopic and can hide in cracks as thin as a credit card. A single female can lay 200-500 eggs in her lifetime, which hatch in 6-10 days under normal conditions.

The biggest challenge is their resistance. Studies from Rutgers University show that modern bed bugs have developed skin thicknesses up to 30% greater than non-resistant strains, making it harder for pesticides to penetrate. They've also developed metabolic resistance, meaning their bodies can break down certain chemicals before those chemicals kill them. This is why the foggers and sprays you find at hardware stores typically fail—they weren't designed to overcome these biological defenses.

Professional treatments work because they use either high heat (which bed bugs cannot resist) or commercial-grade chemicals applied in targeted patterns that force bed bugs out of hiding and into treated zones. Without professional-grade equipment and EPA-restricted products, homeowners are fighting this battle with inadequate tools.

The Two Methods That Actually Work

Research consistently shows two bed bug elimination methods with success rates above 90%: professional heat treatment and targeted professional chemical applications.

Heat treatment raises the temperature in infested rooms to 120-135°F for several hours. Bed bugs and their eggs die at sustained temperatures above 118°F. Professional heat equipment uses specialized heaters and fans to circulate hot air into wall voids, furniture, and other hiding spots. The advantage is single-day treatment, but it requires expensive equipment and careful monitoring to ensure all areas reach lethal temperatures.

Professional chemical treatment uses a combination of EPA-registered insecticides applied in strategic patterns. Unlike store-bought sprays, professional bed bug control in Wichita involves multiple product classes—including residual insecticides, contact killers, and insect growth regulators—applied to baseboards, furniture seams, outlet covers, and other harborage areas. This method typically requires 2-3 treatments spaced 10-14 days apart to catch newly hatched nymphs.

DIY chemical treatments fail 85-95% of the time according to pest management studies. The problem isn't just product strength—it's application technique, coverage patterns, and the bed bugs' ability to detect and avoid improperly applied treatments. When homeowners spray visible areas randomly, bed bugs simply relocate to untreated zones and continue breeding.

What to Expect: Timeline and Preparation

Eliminating bed bugs isn't instant, regardless of method. Heat treatment provides same-day knockdown, but surviving eggs in protected areas can still hatch. Chemical treatments require multiple visits because eggs are resistant to most insecticides—you must kill the nymphs that hatch between treatments.

Before any professional treatment, proper preparation is essential. Remove all bedding, curtains, and clothing from infested rooms and seal them in plastic bags. Wash and dry everything on high heat for at least 30 minutes—dryer heat kills bed bugs at all life stages. Pull furniture away from walls and remove items from closets and drawers. Vacuum thoroughly, especially along baseboards, furniture seams, and carpet edges, then immediately dispose of the vacuum bag outside.

Do not move items from infested rooms to other parts of your home. This spreads the infestation. And don't apply your own pesticides before professional treatment—this can cause bed bugs to scatter into walls and make professional treatment harder.

Professional pest control for bed bugs typically costs $300-$1,500 depending on infestation severity and home size. This seems expensive until you calculate the cost of multiple failed DIY attempts, replaced furniture, lost sleep, and continued bites. Most professional companies offer warranties, meaning if bed bugs return within a certain period, they'll retreat at no charge.

Bed Bug Treatment in Wichita and Surrounding Areas

Wichita's combination of older housing stock and high population mobility (with McConnell Air Force Base nearby) creates conditions where bed bugs can spread quickly through apartment complexes, hotels, and residential neighborhoods. Local pest control companies see increased bed bug calls each year, particularly in multi-family housing where infestations can easily move between units through shared walls and electrical conduits.

If you live in Wichita, El Dorado, Derby, Andover, Augusta, Haysville, Maize, or Goddard, fast response matters. The longer you wait, the larger the infestation grows. A small infestation confined to one bedroom can spread throughout your home in weeks. Working with a locally owned company means faster response times and technicians familiar with the specific challenges Kansas homeowners face—including older homes with more cracks and crevices where bed bugs hide.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can you get rid of bed bugs on your own?

You can eliminate very small, localized bed bug infestations using extreme heat (120°F+ for several hours) and thorough vacuuming, but success rates for DIY elimination drop below 15% once infestations spread beyond a single piece of furniture. Store-bought pesticides rarely work because modern bed bugs have developed resistance to pyrethroids, the active ingredient in most consumer products. Professional treatment is almost always necessary for established infestations.

How long does it take to get rid of bed bugs professionally?

Professional heat treatment can eliminate bed bugs in one day, though follow-up inspections are recommended. Chemical treatments typically require 2-3 applications spaced 10-14 days apart to kill newly hatched nymphs, meaning complete elimination takes 3-5 weeks. Timeline depends on infestation severity, home size, and treatment method selected.

What kills bed bugs instantly?

Direct exposure to temperatures above 118°F kills bed bugs instantly, which is why professional dryers and steamers work on contact. Rubbing alcohol and certain contact pesticides also kill on contact, but they must directly hit the bug and provide no residual protection. Instant-kill methods don't address eggs or hidden bugs, which is why comprehensive treatment requires more than contact killers.

How do you know if bed bugs are gone?

Bed bugs are considered eliminated when you see no live bugs, shed skins, fecal spots, or new bites for at least 60-90 days after treatment. Because eggs can survive treatments and hatch later, and because bed bugs can hide for months between feedings, patience and monitoring are essential. Professional inspections use trained eyes and sometimes detection dogs to confirm elimination.

Will washing clothes kill bed bugs?

Washing clothes in hot water (at least 120°F) followed by 30 minutes in a high-heat dryer kills bed bugs at all life stages, including eggs. The dryer heat is actually more lethal than washing. If items can't be washed, placing them in a dryer on high heat for 30 minutes works. For delicate items, sealing them in plastic bags for 6-12 months will starve any bed bugs inside.

Do bed bugs go away in winter?

Bed bugs do not go away in winter. They live indoors where temperatures remain comfortable year-round. While extreme cold below 0°F can kill bed bugs, indoor heating keeps homes warm enough for bed bugs to remain active throughout Kansas winters. Waiting for seasonal temperature changes to solve a bed bug problem only allows the infestation to grow larger.

Ready to Eliminate Bed Bugs for Good?

Bed bug infestations don't improve on their own—they only grow worse. If you're dealing with bites, sightings, or confirmed bed bugs in your Wichita-area home, professional treatment gives you the highest chance of complete elimination without wasting money on products that don't work.
